A student has finished their 4th semester. They have earned 30 credits from their first year and 25 credits from their second year. Will they be promoted to the 5th semester? Explain the specific credit deficit based on the 108/80/60 rule.

No. The student will **not be promoted to the 5th semester**.

**Why – based on the 108 / 80 / 60 rule**

| Requirement for promotion to Semester 5/6 | Required | Student’s earned |
|--------------------------------------------|----------|------------------|
| **Total earned credits** (by end of Semester IV) | 60 credits | 55 credits |
| **Credits from the first two semesters** | 36 credits | 30 credits |

- **Total credit deficit:** 5 credits short of the required 60.  
- **First‑year credit deficit:** 6 credits short of the required 36 from Sem 1 + Sem 2.

Because both the overall credit minimum (60) **and** the minimum first‑year credit requirement (36) are not met, the student fails the promotion criteria for moving into Semester 5 (or 6).  

(For reference, promotion to Sem 7/8 later requires 108 total credits, with at least 80 from the first four semesters.)
If this is their third time being 'Not Promoted,' what is their last resort to stay in the program, and what is the absolute maximum time they have to graduate?

**Last‑resort option:**  
After the third “Not Promoted” status the student’s name is removed from the faculty rolls. The only way to stay in the program is to file a **Mercy Appeal to the Vice‑Chancellor**. If the appeal is approved, the university may extend the allowed study period.

**Absolute maximum time to graduate:**  
- Normal ceiling: **14 consecutive semesters** (the standard maximum).  
- With a successful Mercy Appeal: the period can be stretched by **up to two additional semesters**, giving an **absolute maximum of 16 semesters** (i.e., eight years).

I am repeating a course this semester because I failed the theory exam last year, but I had 80% attendance back then. If my current attendance drops to 40% due to an internship, can the department detain me from the End-Semester exam?

No. Because you already satisfied the attendance requirement (80 %) when you first took the course, the “repeating‑students exemption” applies: you will not be detained for low attendance in the repeat semester, even though your current attendance is only 40 %.  

You may therefore register the repeated theory course in **Mode B** (appear in all evaluation components) or **Mode C** (appear only for the end‑semester exam), as the repetition rules allow for either mode when the theory exam was failed but attendance was previously completed.
Since I'm repeating this theory course and already fulfilled attendance, which registration modes (b or c) are available to me, and how do they differ regarding sessional marks?

**Registration modes you can use**

| Mode | What you appear in | How sessional marks are treated |
|------|-------------------|---------------------------------|
| **Mode B** | All evaluation components (theory‑sessionals, practicals, end‑semester exam). | Sessionals are taken **again**; the new sessional marks replace the previous ones for that attempt. |
| **Mode C** | End‑semester exam only. | The **previous** sessional marks you earned earlier are retained and counted toward the final grade; you only sit the end‑semester exam again. |

Because you failed the theory exam but had already satisfied the attendance requirement, you are eligible to register the repeated course in **either Mode B or Mode C**. Choose Mode B if you want a chance to improve the sessional component, or Mode C if you prefer to keep the earlier sessional score and only retake the final exam.

I am a first-year student with a CGPA of 7.8. I passed all my exams, but I was absent for one mid-term (Internal Exam). Can I apply for a branch change? What are the specific constraints that might prevent my transfer even if I meet the merit criteria?

Yes – with a CGPA of 7.8 and having cleared every first‑year course, you satisfy the basic eligibility for a branch change (the rule requires CGPA ≥ 7.5 and all first‑year courses passed).

**Constraints that can still block the transfer**

| Constraint | What it means for you |
|------------|-----------------------|
| **Seat availability** | A vacancy must exist in the desired branch; if all seats are filled, the change cannot be granted. |
| **Original‑branch strength** | The transfer must not reduce the student count in your current branch below 70 % of its approved intake. |
| **Attendance requirement** | You must have met the minimum attendance (≥ 75 %) for each course, or have obtained a condonation (65‑74 % with committee approval). If the missed mid‑term caused your attendance to fall below the required level and no condonation is granted, the branch‑change request will be rejected. |
| **Application timing** | Requests are only accepted after the completion of the first two semesters (i.e., after the II‑semester results are declared). |
| **Academic standing** | Any disciplinary action, detention, or pending fee dues can disqualify you, even if the CGPA and results are satisfactory. |
| **Merit ranking** | Branch changes are allotted strictly on merit; if other candidates have higher CGPA or better rank, you may not get the desired seat. |

If you meet all the above conditions—especially the attendance/condonation rule and the availability/strength limits—your branch‑change application can be processed successfully.
If the branch I want to join is popular and many people are leaving my current branch, at what point does the University legally have to stop allowing transfers out of my department?

The university must stop permitting transfers out of your current branch as soon as the number of students remaining would bring the branch’s strength below **70 % of its approved intake**.  

In practice, this works like this:

| Situation | Action required |
|-----------|-----------------|
| **Current enrollment = X** (approved intake) | The branch can lose up to **30 % × X** students and still stay at the 70 % threshold. |
| **Students already approved for transfer = Y** | If **Y ≥ 0.30 × X**, the remaining strength would be ≤ 70 % of the intake, so **no further transfers** can be authorized. |
| **Additional transfer request arrives** | The university checks the projected remaining strength. If granting the request would push the strength **below 70 %**, the request must be **rejected**. |

**Example**  
- Approved intake for a branch = 100 students.  
- 30 % of 100 = 30 students can leave.  
- If 28 students have already transferred out, the branch still has 72 % of its seats (72 students) and can allow up to 2 more transfers.  
- The 31st transfer would reduce the strength to 69 students (69 % of intake), which is below the legal limit, so the university must stop further transfers at that point.  

Thus, the legal stop point is reached **the moment the projected post‑transfer enrollment would fall under 70 % of the branch’s sanctioned intake**.
